title: Printing and Comments
description: println versus print, escape sequences for quotes and tabs, and notes that Java ignores.

content.value: There are two printing instructions and the difference is one letter. `System.out.println(...)` prints and then moves to a new line. `System.out.print(...)` prints and stays exactly where it is, so the next thing printed continues on the same line.
Four instructions, two lines of output. The three `print` calls built up one line between them, and the `println` at the end of it finished that line off.
`print` is what you want when you ask someone a question and expect them to type on the same line. You will use it for exactly that in Module 3.
Inside a print you can join pieces of text with `+`. Java sticks them together in order, with no extra spaces, so any space you want has to be inside the quotes.

The third line shows something useful: a number joined to text becomes part of the text. Java turns the `4` into the characters `4` for you. In Module 2 you will see when that is a help and when it catches people out.

A piece of text starts and ends with a double quote, so how do you print a double quote? You escape it: write `\"` and Java prints the quote instead of ending the text. The backslash means "treat the next character specially".
Three escapes are worth memorising now. `\n` is a new line, `\t` is a tab, and `\\` is a single backslash. Everything else you can look up when you need it.
`\n` inside a `print` and a `println` do the same job. Use whichever keeps your code easiest to read: one `println` with `\n` in it, or two separate `println` calls.

A comment is a note for humans. Java skips it completely, so you can write anything you like. Start a one line comment with `//`, and everything to the end of that line is a note. For several lines, open with `/*` and close with `*/`.
Look at that last line. Putting `//` in front of a real instruction switches it off without deleting it. That is called commenting out, and it is how programmers test which line is causing a problem.

Write comments to explain why you did something, not what the line says. `// add 1 to score` is noise next to `score = score + 1`. `// bonus point for a fast answer` tells the next reader something the code cannot.

practice.question: Use two `print` calls and one `println` so the output is exactly one line reading: Java is fun!
Print this exactly, quotes included: My teacher said "well done" today.
Print a two line shopping list using a single `println` with `\n` in the middle: Bread on the first line, Milk on the second. Add a comment above it saying what it is.

quiz.question: What does `System.out.print` do differently from `System.out.println`?
options: It does not move to a new line afterwards.
quiz.explain: `print` leaves the cursor on the same line, so the next output continues it. The `ln` in `println` is the new line.

quiz.question: What does this print?  `System.out.println("Game" + "Over");`
quiz.explain: `+` joins the pieces with nothing in between. A space has to be written inside the quotes: `"Game" + " " + "Over"`.

quiz.question: How do you print a double quote inside a piece of text?
options: Use two double quotes in a row.
You cannot print a double quote.
quiz.explain: The backslash tells Java the next character is part of the text rather than the end of it, so `\"` prints a quote.

quiz.question: What happens to a line starting with `//`?
options: Java prints it as a message.
quiz.explain: `//` starts a comment: a note for people reading the code. The compiler skips straight past it.

quiz.question: Which escape sequence starts a new line?
quiz.explain: `\n` is a new line, `\t` is a tab, and `\\` prints a single backslash.
